paragraphs: The paper studies how to audit a prediction system for data minimization when its internal workings are hidden. Its central question is whether each input feature is individually necessary for the task. The proposed test replaces a feature with a constant across prediction instances and measures how much the outputs change.

This output instability becomes a metric for data minimization. The authors then use a Bayesian approach to move from measurements on a finite sample to a probabilistic guarantee about a distribution. That distinction matters because an audit usually observes only some inputs, while its conclusions concern the system more broadly.

The paper also addresses limited access to the prediction service. It treats the allocation of queries across candidate imputations as a bandit problem, developing algorithms for deciding whether a target minimization level holds and for measuring minimization under a fixed budget. Experiments on real prediction systems show substantial improvements over simpler benchmarks for both auditing tasks.
neurips-2021-auditing-black-box-predicti.tldr: The paper audits black-box data minimization by testing constant feature replacements and allocating limited queries to obtain probabilistic guarantees.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn a sequence of tasks while retaining what it learned earlier. A central difficulty is catastrophic forgetting: learning a new task can damage performance on previous ones. This paper argues that preserving earlier knowledge is only part of the objective; a learner should also use relevant experience to help with later tasks.

BNS addresses these two goals by dynamically building a network for each new task. Network construction is therefore part of the learning process, with the stated purpose of both overcoming forgetting and transferring knowledge across tasks. The approach treats retention and reuse as goals to pursue together.

The experiments distinguish tasks with little shared knowledge from tasks that have more in common. BNS outperforms the reported state-of-the-art baselines even in the former setting. Its advantage is substantially larger when tasks share knowledge, which the authors attribute to transfer. These findings support the value of evaluating continual learners on their ability to reuse knowledge as well as preserve it.
neurips-2021-bns-building-network-struct.tldr: BNS dynamically builds networks for successive tasks to address forgetting and transfer knowledge, with larger reported gains when tasks share knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether useful training examples can be identified before a neural network has completed training. On standard vision datasets, the authors find that simple scores computed early and averaged across several weight initializations can identify examples that matter for generalization. This makes data selection possible without observing the entire training trajectory.

The proposed scores are GraNd, based on gradient norms, and EL2N, based on the size of prediction errors. Across the evaluated architectures and datasets, these scores support removing substantial portions of training data without reducing test accuracy. In one example, EL2N measured after a few epochs permits removing half of CIFAR10's training set while slightly improving test accuracy.

For a given dataset, EL2N scores also transfer across architectures or hyperparameter configurations. The authors additionally use the scores to detect noisy examples and examine how data shapes training dynamics and learned representations. Together, the findings present early training behavior as a useful signal for both selecting data and studying its influence.
neurips-2021-deep-learning-on-a-data-die.tldr: Simple scores measured early in training identify useful examples and enable substantial data pruning without sacrificing test accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: N:M pruning retains N nonzero weights in each group of M weights. This structure is attractive for sparse neural networks, but applying the same sparsity pattern to every layer can cause substantial accuracy losses at high sparsity. DominoSearch investigates whether allowing layers to use different N:M schemes improves the accuracy available under a fixed resource budget.

The method searches for mixed schemes starting from pretrained dense networks. Its comparisons hold constraints such as model size or operation count equal, so the reported benefits concern how sparsity is allocated across layers. On ImageNet, a ResNet18 with 2.1 million parameters and 87.5% sparsity improves top-1 accuracy by 2.1 percentage points over its uniform counterpart.

At a matched budget of 227 million FLOPs, the reported ResNet18 improvement is 1.3 percentage points. A sparse ResNet50 reaches 76.7% top-1 accuracy with 5 million parameters, competitive with the cited layer-wise unstructured pruning results. These findings support mixed N:M patterns as a promising structured compression approach and motivate further hardware and algorithm co-design.
neurips-2021-dominosearch-find-layer-wis.tldr: DominoSearch varies N:M sparsity across layers to improve reported accuracy over uniform sparsity at matched model-size or computation budgets.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a learning problem in which feedback compares whole teams rather than individual players. Each duel involves two disjoint teams of k players drawn from n available players. The learner seeks a Condorcet winning team: one whose probability of winning against every disjoint opponent is at least one half.

The challenge is to identify such a team with high probability using few comparisons. The model links noisy comparison outcomes to a total ordering of teams. For stochastic feedback, the authors reduce the problem to classical dueling bandits and derive a comparison bound depending on the number of players, team size, and a gap parameter. Its inverse-square dependence on that gap makes the guarantee sensitive to how distinguishable the comparisons are.

For deterministic feedback, the paper provides an additional algorithm with a bound of order nk log k plus k to the fifth power, independent of a gap parameter. The contribution establishes algorithms and comparison guarantees for collective choices when observations arrive only through team-level contests.
neurips-2021-dueling-bandits-with-team-c.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and comparison guarantees for identifying a winning team from noisy or deterministic contests between disjoint teams.

paragraphs: Generative radiance fields distribute training gradients throughout a volume, which helps optimization but can leave object surfaces diffuse. Occupancy representations offer definite surfaces, yet using them directly concentrates gradients on those surfaces and can make training fail to converge. This paper addresses the tension between learning reliably and recovering well-defined geometry.

Generative Occupancy Fields begin with the broader rendering behavior of radiance fields and progressively move toward surface-based rendering. As the learned surface becomes more accurate, the method shrinks the region sampled during rendering, moving from the full volume to a small neighborhood around the surface. This staged transition connects the training advantages of one representation with the geometric advantages of the other.

Experiments across multiple datasets show high-quality synthesized images with 3D consistency alongside compact, smooth surfaces. The findings indicate that surface formation and successful generative training can be pursued together through a gradual rendering transition. The contribution is therefore about both the resulting images and the object geometry learned while producing them.
neurips-2021-generative-occupancy-fields.tldr: Generative Occupancy Fields gradually concentrate rendering near learned surfaces to produce 3D-consistent images and compact geometry without impeding convergence.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search usually evaluates candidate networks through a particular downstream task. GenNAS asks whether a more general test can assess an architecture's ability to capture and transform input patterns. It evaluates networks using regression against manually designed synthetic signals, without requiring task-specific labels for this basic evaluation.

The synthetic regression task serves as a proxy for downstream performance. Experiments cover thirteen convolutional-network search spaces and one language-processing search space. They assess both training speed and how well the proxy ranks architectures compared with their downstream results. On NAS-Bench-101, the reported ranking correlation is 0.85, compared with 0.38 for the existing efficient methods discussed in the abstract.

The paper also introduces an automatic search for combinations of synthetic signals, using a limited amount of downstream labeled data to improve performance further. End-to-end evaluations report strong results and significant speedups across the search spaces, including near-optimal architectures on NASBench-201 within 0.3 GPU hour. The findings support synthetic regression as an efficient architecture-evaluation signal.
neurips-2021-generic-neural-architecture.tldr: GenNAS uses synthetic-signal regression to evaluate architectures efficiently, with strong reported agreement between its rankings and downstream performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies which matrix an optimization algorithm selects when several matrices minimize the same empirical loss. It examines discrete-time mirror descent for matrix sensing without adding an explicit regularization penalty. The central issue is implicit regularization: the algorithm's own structure can favor particular solutions even when the objective does not specify that preference.

Using an analysis based on Bregman divergence, the authors characterize convergence for rectangular matrices and positive semidefinite matrices under different mirror maps. Among global loss minimizers, the selected matrix minimizes a quantity explicitly connected to nuclear norm, Frobenius norm, and von Neumann entropy. This characterization yields low-rank recovery under the same assumptions sufficient for nuclear-norm minimization.

The paper also connects mirror descent to gradient descent on a full-rank factorization when the sensing matrices are symmetric and commute. Under those conditions, factorized gradient descent is a first-order approximation to mirror descent. The connection additionally provides an explicit description of gradient flow's implicit bias, linking algorithm choice to the structure of recovered solutions.
neurips-2021-implicit-regularization-in-.tldr: The paper characterizes mirror descent's implicit preference among matrix-sensing solutions and proves low-rank recovery under assumptions sufficient for nuclear-norm minimization.

paragraphs: The paper treats exploration as a skill that can accumulate across environments. Instead of learning how to explore separately from scratch in each setting, an agent first trains across multiple environments without an external task goal. It later transfers its exploration policy to new environments while solving tasks, making previous exploration experience part of the evaluation.

The proposed approach combines two sources of exploratory motivation. One depends on the agent's beliefs and encourages visiting parts of the environment it has not seen. The other depends on the environment and encourages attention to inherently interesting objects. Together, these components account for both what remains unfamiliar to the agent and what in the scene attracts exploration.

The authors compare several exploration strategies and report that their formulation produces the most consistent exploration across the tested training–testing environment pairs. They also introduce benchmarks and evaluation metrics for this transfer setting. The findings support studying exploration through reusable policies, with performance judged partly by how well exploratory behavior carries into new environments.
neurips-2021-interesting-object-curious-.tldr: The paper learns transferable exploration policies by combining the pursuit of unseen places with interest in objects across environments.

paragraphs: Learning a policy through environmental interaction can require many samples. This paper focuses on local policy search, where random perturbations are often used to estimate a direction for improvement. Such samples can produce high-variance gradient estimates. The authors investigate whether actively choosing informative evaluations can make that local search more sample-efficient.

Their algorithm builds a probabilistic model of both the objective function and its gradient. It uses that model to decide where to request a noisy objective evaluation, choosing queries to improve the gradient estimate. Although the feedback provides objective values rather than derivatives, the accumulated observations inform which direction the policy search should take next.

This combines Bayesian optimization's active sampling with gradient-based local search. Comparisons with existing black-box algorithms on synthetic objectives show lower variance and improved sample complexity in the reported evaluations. Experiments on reinforcement-learning benchmarks further illustrate benefits from active sampling. The contribution is a way to make individual evaluations more informative for the local optimization step.
neurips-2021-local-policy-search-with-ba.tldr: The method actively selects objective evaluations using a probabilistic model to improve gradient estimates for local policy search.

paragraphs: Single-image internal learning trains a generator using the statistics of one image, allowing it to produce new images from that example. Training each model on only one image limits the framework's scale and applications. This paper introduces meta-learning across an image collection so that individual image models can benefit from shared features.

A convolutional feedforward hypernetwork takes an input image and generates its single-image GAN model. The generated model includes a hierarchy of generators and discriminators, so training the hypernetwork itself requires an adversarial approach. The authors support their design choices with theoretical analysis. Sharing this model-generating network also makes interpolation between generative models possible.

The reported results show that the generated models remain suitable for many common applications served by single-image GANs, while substantially reducing training time per image without losing performance. The approach also enables feedforward modeling of new images and interpolation. Its central contribution is to learn how to construct image-specific generative models using experience gathered across images.
neurips-2021-meta-internal-learning-4ca4.tldr: A hypernetwork learns across images to generate single-image GANs, reducing per-image training time while enabling interpolation and feedforward modeling.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional object detection from point clouds often requires complex training and testing pipelines with substantial dataset-specific knowledge. Object DGCNN proposes an architecture that predicts a set of objects through message passing on a dynamic graph. It extends the DGCNN framework from its existing formulation to the task of object-set prediction.

The construction removes the need for post-processing through object-confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. These operations would otherwise be additional stages in producing the final detections. The paper therefore addresses the organization of the detection pipeline as well as the underlying prediction model, following the inspiration of suppression-free approaches to two-dimensional detection.

To help with sparse point clouds, the authors also introduce set-to-set knowledge distillation. Teacher and student outputs are aligned without depending on their ordering, matching the fact that detections form a set. The method achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on autonomous-driving benchmarks. Analyses of both detection and distillation accompany the results, supporting the proposed combination of direct object-set prediction and order-independent knowledge transfer.
neurips-2021-object-dgcnn-3d-object-dete.tldr: Object DGCNN predicts 3D object sets through dynamic graphs and uses order-independent distillation to support detection from sparse point clouds.

paragraphs: Federated learning repeatedly gathers updates from selected clients to train a shared model. This paper examines cohort size: the number of clients selected in each round. It asks how increasing that number affects both the quality of the resulting model and the behavior of training, rather than treating greater participation as an automatically beneficial scaling choice.

The study connects this question to large-batch training in centralized learning. Its empirical evaluation identifies parallels, including generalization problems and diminishing returns. These findings indicate that increasing the amount of participation per round can bring familiar optimization and performance tradeoffs even though the updates come from separate clients.

The authors also identify challenges they distinguish as specific to federated learning, including catastrophic training failures and fairness concerns. They investigate how methods might use larger cohorts effectively, while describing their answers as partial. The work frames cohort size as an algorithmic design choice with consequences beyond aggregate training progress, including whether benefits are distributed fairly.
neurips-2021-on-large-cohort-training-fo.tldr: An empirical study finds that larger federated-learning cohorts introduce generalization, diminishing-return, training-failure, and fairness challenges.

paragraphs: Few-shot meta-learning aims to adapt a model to unfamiliar classes using only a small set of labeled examples. Those adaptation examples are called support data. This paper examines how much the choice of that small set can influence the resulting predictions, even when the examples themselves are ordinary images from the expected data distribution.

The authors demonstrate support images that lead modern meta-learning algorithms to accuracies as low as 4% or as high as 95% on standard few-shot image-classification benchmarks. The images are natural and unmodified. The result establishes that extreme sensitivity can arise from which valid examples are provided for adaptation, without needing altered or out-of-distribution inputs.

The paper explains these empirical observations in terms of class margins, which describe separation between classes. Its analysis suggests that robust and safe meta-learning needs larger margins than supervised learning. This is a proposed implication of the observed sensitivity: successful few-shot adaptation depends not only on learning quickly, but also on remaining reliable across choices of support data.
neurips-2021-on-sensitivity-of-meta-lear.tldr: Natural support-image choices can cause extreme accuracy differences in few-shot meta-learning, with class-margin analysis suggesting stronger separation is needed for robustness.

paragraphs: Fully estimating an unknown quantum state's entries requires exponentially many copies as the number of qubits grows. Weaker learning models can instead learn approximate information using linearly many copies. This paper asks how several such models relate, including private learning, online learning, and approaches that learn selected information about a state.

The authors prove information-theoretic implications from differentially private PAC learning to online learning and then to quantum stability, a concept introduced in the paper. They extend techniques from Boolean-valued learning to real-valued learning and quantum states. A central ingredient is the Robust Standard Optimal Algorithm, a quantum online learner designed to tolerate adversarial imprecision.

The work also establishes connections involving one-way communication, combinatorial parameters, and quantum-state learnability. Further applications concern gentle shadow tomography and learning with noise. These results explain how capabilities in one learning framework can imply capabilities in another. Because the stated connections are information-theoretic, their contribution concerns what learning is possible across these models.
neurips-2021-private-learning-implies-qu.tldr: The paper proves information-theoretic connections from private quantum-state learning to online learning and quantum stability using an imprecision-robust learner.

paragraphs: Many private query-answering methods reconstruct a discrete data distribution from noisy measurements. This reconstruction can make answers mutually consistent and reduce error, but representing the distribution may require space that grows exponentially with the number of variables. The paper addresses this computational obstacle within the PRIVATE-PGM approach.

PRIVATE-PGM represents the distribution through a graphical model whose structure depends on which variables occur together in the measurements. Its computational demands follow the difficulty of exact marginal inference in that graph. Sparse measurements can therefore be handled efficiently, while dense measurements in high dimensions can make the method unable to run.

The proposed solution relaxes consistency constraints in the estimation objective. This changes the reconstruction problem so that the main scalability barrier can be reduced. The approach is compatible with many existing private query-answering algorithms and provides improvements in scalability or accuracy without additional privacy cost. Its significance is that the reconstruction stage can be made more practical while retaining the underlying privacy budget.
neurips-2021-relaxed-marginal-consistenc.tldr: Relaxing reconstruction consistency constraints improves the scalability or accuracy of private query answering without additional privacy cost.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must improve behavior while accounting for the consequences of exploration. The paper identifies a practical difficulty with earlier methods that offer safety guarantees under regularity assumptions: applying them to large problems has been challenging. It introduces SPO-LF as an approach to policy optimization using information locally available from sensors.

SPO-LF learns the relationship between those local features and environmental reward and safety through generalized linear function approximations. Policy improvement and learning these relationships occur together. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for safety and optimality, making the treatment of safety part of the algorithm's analysis as well as its empirical evaluation.

The experiments report lower sample requirements and computational costs, along with greater applicability to large problems, compared with previous safe reinforcement-learning methods that provide theoretical guarantees. Against advanced deep reinforcement-learning methods with safety constraints, SPO-LF is reported to have comparable sample efficiency and better safety. These comparisons support local feature-based modeling as a useful route toward practical safe policy optimization in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-safe-policy-optimization-wi.tldr: SPO-LF learns reward and safety from local sensor features, combining theoretical guarantees with reported efficiency and safety improvements.

paragraphs: Large training batches support extensive parallel computation, but they can come at a cost to generalization. Existing adaptive approaches may change batch size only at coarse intervals because their calculations are expensive or require manual tuning. SimiGrad proposes an automated, lightweight way to adjust batch size at finer intervals, potentially every mini-batch.

Its central component is an efficient representation of important gradient-noise information, with gradient similarity providing the method's organizing idea. The goal is to make frequent adaptation affordable enough for large-scale training. The authors also provide the methodology as a plugin supporting mainstream machine-learning frameworks, connecting the proposed batching strategy to practical training workflows.

Evaluations on CIFAR10, ImageNet, and BERT-Large report improvements over adaptive and manually tuned static batching approaches in both performance and supported batch size. For BERT-Large pretraining, the method uses a batch size of 78,000 with a SQuAD score of 90.69, compared with the cited previous result of 90.58 at 59,000. These findings support finer-grained adaptation in the tested workloads.
neurips-2021-simigrad-fine-grained-adapt.tldr: SimiGrad uses lightweight gradient information to adapt batch sizes frequently, enabling larger batches with strong reported model performance.

paragraphs: Piano transcription aims to recover note events from audio, including the intervals during which notes occur. Many systems first predict pitch activity frame by frame and then assemble those predictions into notes through heuristics. Others estimate different stages of a note independently. This paper argues for optimizing the complete note event directly.

The proposed formulation uses a neural semi-Markov conditional random field, or semi-CRF. Its output layer scores intervals instead of individual frames, aligning the prediction unit with the desired note event. This avoids relying on separate frame-level estimates for the different stages of each note and changes how the transcription objective represents the task.

Experiments on MAESTRO show performance above the reported state of the art. The authors describe the output layer as simple and fast in their results, while acknowledging that its complexity remains quadratic. They also suggest that event-based prediction could benefit other areas currently organized around frame-level estimates. That broader possibility extends the motivation, while the demonstrated result concerns piano transcription.
neurips-2021-skipping-the-frame-level-ev.tldr: A neural semi-CRF predicts whole piano-note intervals directly and surpasses the reported state of the art on MAESTRO.

paragraphs: The paper considers stochastic nonconvex optimization where the objective averages smooth loss functions. The target is an approximate stationary point, meaning a point with a small gradient. Existing variance-reduction techniques achieve tight convergence rates, but maintaining reference points and choosing very large batch sizes can create a difficult tuning problem.

Recursive momentum offers a way to avoid those reference points and large batches. The earlier STORM method uses this idea while retaining the optimal rate, but it requires knowledge of smoothness and a bound on gradient norms. STORM+ builds on that approach with a new mechanism for adapting both the learning rate and momentum parameters.

The resulting method is described as completely parameter-free and does not require large batches. It achieves the optimal convergence rate of order one over T to the one-third power for finding an approximate stationary point in the stated setting. The contribution is to retain that theoretical rate while removing the parameter knowledge and tuning requirements highlighted for earlier approaches.
neurips-2021-storm-fully-adaptive-sgd-wi.tldr: STORM+ adaptively sets learning rate and recursive momentum, achieving the stated optimal stationary-point convergence rate without tuning parameters or large batches.

paragraphs: A neural ODE repeatedly evaluates a neural network during numerical integration. Ordinary backpropagation consumes memory proportional to the number of evaluations multiplied by network size, including when checkpointing splits the computation into smaller pieces. An adjoint method reduces memory by integrating backward in time, but controlling its numerical errors can require substantial computation.

This paper proposes a symplectic adjoint method, using a symplectic integrator to compute the adjoint. The method obtains the exact gradient up to rounding error while using memory proportional to the number of network evaluations plus the network size. Replacing multiplicative memory dependence with additive dependence is central to its stated computational advantage.

The experiments report much lower memory use than naive backpropagation and checkpointing, faster execution than the compared adjoint method, and greater robustness to rounding errors. These findings connect the mathematical gradient property with practical training costs. The result addresses a specific tradeoff in neural ODE learning: preserving gradient accuracy while reducing the memory and computation needed to obtain it.
neurips-2021-symplectic-adjoint-method-f.tldr: The symplectic adjoint method computes neural ODE gradients exactly up to rounding error with additive memory scaling and reported efficiency gains.

paragraphs: SATNet connects a differentiable logical solver with neural networks, allowing systems to learn visual reasoning tasks such as Sudoku from images. A major obstacle is symbol grounding: establishing how visual inputs correspond to the symbolic variables used for reasoning. Earlier success depended on explicit intermediate supervision, creating a label-leakage concern.

The paper introduces a self-supervised pretraining pipeline that enables SATNet to handle this mapping without intermediate labels. This expands the range of datasets to which the architecture can be applied. The change targets the connection between perception and logical reasoning, which must work for the solver to reason correctly about what it sees.

The authors demonstrate full accuracy in a harder experimental setup designed to prevent label leakage. They also introduce a proofreading method that further improves SATNet architectures and exceeds the reported state of the art on Visual Sudoku. These findings show that the proposed training pipeline can overcome the demonstrated grounding barrier, with proofreading providing an additional improvement in the evaluated visual reasoning task.
neurips-2021-techniques-for-symbol-groun.tldr: Self-supervised pretraining enables SATNet to ground visual symbols without intermediate labels, while proofreading further improves Visual Sudoku performance.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a single learning approach for episodic decision problems that performs well under two different loss regimes. With adversarial losses, the target regret grows roughly with the square root of the number of episodes, ignoring logarithmic factors. With almost-stochastic losses, the target is logarithmic regret. The challenge is obtaining both guarantees when the fixed transition dynamics are unknown.

The authors work within the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader framework. They first introduce a loss-shifting technique that simplifies the analysis for known transitions and improves the corresponding results. They then extend the idea to the harder setting where the learner must also estimate how actions lead to subsequent states.

The key new analysis bounds transition-estimation error using regret itself in the stochastic setting. This connection is what enables the logarithmic guarantee despite uncertainty about the transitions. The paper thereby resolves the stated open problem, combining protection against adversarial losses with stronger performance guarantees when the losses have the more favorable almost-stochastic structure.
neurips-2021-the-best-of-both-worlds-sto.tldr: The paper achieves adversarial and almost-stochastic regret guarantees for episodic decision processes with unknown fixed transitions.

paragraphs: An interpolating model fits its training observations exactly, yet it can sometimes still predict well on new data. This paper studies that phenomenon in high-dimensional linear regression with Gaussian data. It asks how generalization guarantees based on the size or geometry of a hypothesis class can explain such benign overfitting.

The authors prove a uniform bound for interpolators in an arbitrary hypothesis class, expressed through the class's Gaussian width. Applying it to Euclidean norm balls recovers an existing consistency result for minimum-norm interpolators. It also confirms a prediction about interpolators whose norms are close to minimal, specifically in the Gaussian-data setting considered here.

A further application to the simplex yields a new consistency result for minimum l1-norm interpolation, also called basis pursuit. These applications demonstrate that one general bound can address different restrictions on fitted models. The conclusion is qualified: norm-based generalization bounds can explain benign overfitting in some settings, with the paper's guarantees developed under its Gaussian linear-regression assumptions.
neurips-2021-uniform-convergence-of-inte.tldr: A Gaussian-width generalization bound explains benign overfitting for several norm-constrained interpolators in Gaussian linear regression.

paragraphs: Switching dynamical systems describe processes whose behavior changes between regimes while their state evolves over time. This paper develops a continuous-time model, motivated by applications such as biology and discrete-event systems. A Markov jump process determines regime changes and modulates a diffusion process describing the evolving continuous state.

The authors derive exact equations for the prior and posterior marginal densities, but solving them directly is computationally intractable. They therefore introduce a variational inference algorithm that combines a Gaussian-process approximation for the diffusion with posterior inference for the jump process. The approximation is obtained by minimizing a path-wise Kullback–Leibler divergence, addressing the behavior of trajectories over time.

The resulting method provides Bayesian estimates of latent states at arbitrary time points and point estimates of unknown system parameters through variational expectation maximization. It is evaluated both under the model assumptions and on real-world examples. The contribution makes inference practical for the proposed continuous-time switching model while retaining estimates of hidden states and learning its unknown parameters.
neurips-2021-variational-inference-for-c.tldr: The paper develops variational inference for continuous-time switching systems, estimating hidden states and unknown parameters when exact inference is intractable.
